name: Bianca Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-year apprentice on a connections crew in Fernbrook, which is basically a commuter town that keeps growing new housing estates. So my days are hooking new streets up to the network, putting in streetlights, and fixing whatever the diggers hit, which is a lot. I keep a little notebook in my top pocket with everything Dev, my crew leader, tells me, because I'm still slower than I want to be. The best bit is switching on a new street at dusk and watching all the porch lights come on at once.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Early starts and tight money. Marco, my fiancé, drives a delivery van, and we're trying to save for a wedding next autumn on two low wages, so right now we've got about two weeks of money in the bank. And there's no other line company within an hour, so if this job went, I'd be starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, one less thing to worry about. At work we'd probably laugh about all the people who said we'd be replaced. Online I'd maybe share a funny post and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's the best case, honestly. I finish my apprenticeship, the pay goes up, the wedding happens. I'd keep using AI for the odd report, but that's all it is to me anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick with the plan in my notebook: qualify in eighteen months, save fifty a week for the wedding. Maybe pick up streetlight call-outs at weekends for the overtime. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit relieved. It means the plan I've written down still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly writing up incident reports, because I'm not good at the formal language and Dev hates paperwork. I tell it what happened and it tidies it up. I always read it back, because once it made a near-miss sound like nothing happened at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the plan in your notebook.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Back page is money: rent, van insurance for Marco, wedding fund, and a line called emergency that's mostly empty. Front pages are knots, clearances, things Dev says twice. I'm a list person, it calms me down.

S0.say: She'd say fine, one less thing to worry about, and laugh at work about the people who predicted replacement. Online she'd share a joke and move on.
S0.think: It's her best case: she qualifies, her pay rises and the wedding goes ahead. She'd keep using AI for the odd report, which is all it is to her anyway.
S0.do: Sticks to her written plan: qualify in eighteen months and save fifty a week for the wedding. Picks up weekend streetlight call-outs for overtime.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved that her written plan still works.
S0.quote: Back page is money: rent, van insurance for Marco, wedding fund, and a line called emergency that's mostly empty.
S0.fieldNote: She manages worry through lists, and her notebook makes her finances very concrete, including an emergency line that is mostly empty. She uses AI cautiously for reports and has caught it softening a near-miss. Her calm depends on her plan staying intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense to get ready and not panic. Some jobs change, some don't, and the people who learn the new stuff will be fine. I'd probably tell Marco the same thing, a bit too often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm more worried for Marco than me. Delivery vans that drive themselves feel a lot closer than a robot that can splice a cable on a muddy estate. If his job goes, our wedding fund and my rent share go with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see which tools the company actually brings in, then learn them properly once a couple of the crew are using them. I'd move more of the wedding money into the emergency line, maybe half. And I'd sit down with Marco and look at what he could do if driving dried up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More of a worry for us as a couple than for me on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if Marco's job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big wedding, without even thinking. We'd do the registry office and a barbecue at my parents'. I'd be sad for about a day and then I'd be glad we didn't spend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see which tools come in. Why not get ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen the company buy stuff and drop it within a year, like the tablets for site checks. I don't want to spend evenings learning something that'll be in a cupboard by summer. Once Dev's using it, I'll learn it fast.

S1.say: It makes sense to get ready without panicking, since some jobs change and people who learn the new things will be fine. She'd tell Marco the same, perhaps too often.
S1.think: She worries more for Marco, because self-driving delivery vans seem closer than robots splicing cable on muddy estates. If his job goes, the wedding fund and his rent share go too.
S1.do: Learns new company tools properly once a couple of crew members use them. Moves about half the wedding money into the emergency fund and sits down with Marco to look at his options beyond driving.
S1.feel: Uneasy, more worried for them as a couple than for herself.
S1.quote: I don't want to spend evenings learning something that'll be in a cupboard by summer.
S1.fieldNote: Her risk is mostly household risk: Marco's driving job looks more exposed than her line work. Her steady adaptability is grounded in experience of the company dropping tools like the site tablets. She'd downsize the wedding readily and with little regret.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and somebody needs to slow it down or at least catch people. I'm not a big politics person, but two years is just not fair on anyone. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's both of us at once, me and Marco, with two weeks of savings. I'd still be an apprentice when it hit, and the van would be driving itself. I honestly don't know what we'd live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd put the wedding off, simple as that, and cut down to rent, food and phones. I'd ask my parents if we could move into their back room for a while, which they'd say yes to before I finished asking. I'd keep working every hour they'd give me until the day they didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd probably be making lists at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be on that two-in-the-morning list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What we owe, what we can sell, what my parents can lend without it hurting them. Marco's guitar would be on there, which he'd hate. Then a line at the bottom that says what now, with nothing under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the speed change your plans compared to the slower ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely, because with two years there's no point starting a course, it'd be out of date before I finished. It's just survive and see. With more time, I'd actually plan something.

S2.say: It's too fast, and someone needs to slow it down or at least catch people. She isn't political, but she'd say two years is not fair on anyone.
S2.think: Both she and Marco would be hit at once with two weeks of savings, her still an apprentice and his van driving itself. She doesn't know what they'd live on.
S2.do: Postpones the wedding and cuts down to rent, food and phones. Moves with Marco into her parents' back room and works every hour offered until the work stops.
S2.feel: Alarmed, making lists at two in the morning.
S2.quote: Then a line at the bottom that says what now, with nothing under it.
S2.fieldNote: Her habit of list-making turns into a picture of distress: a list ending with what now and nothing under it. With two years she sees no point retraining and switches to survival. Her parents are a reliable safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's enough to get sensible about it. Companies and the government should be planning now, and people should start looking at their options. I'd say it calmly, because panicking helps nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I qualify, I'd get a few years on proper pay, and we'd probably still have the wedding. But I'd be planning for what comes after, because the job ends either way. Marco's probably goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, then look at something like electrical inspection or safety checking, where a person has to sign off. I'd pick it once I'd seen other people go that way and it worked for them. We'd make the wedding small and put the difference into savings, and we'd hold off on kids until we knew where we stood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an anxious I can work with. I'd have a list and a timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which of the older crew leave and where they go, and whether they're happy there. If Dev went to inspections and liked it, I'd follow him. I trust people more than predictions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned holding off on kids. Was that in the plan before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about it maybe three years after the wedding. In this one I'd push it back, because I wouldn't want to have a baby the year both our jobs disappeared. It's not a happy thing to say, but it's honest.

S3.say: Five years is short but enough to get sensible: companies and government should plan now and people should look at their options. She'd say it calmly, because panic helps nobody.
S3.think: She'd qualify, get a few years on proper pay and still have the wedding, but she'd plan for afterwards because the job ends either way. Marco's likely goes first.
S3.do: Finishes the apprenticeship, then moves towards electrical inspection or safety checking once she's seen others do it successfully. Has a small wedding, saves the difference and delays having children.
S3.feel: Anxious but workable, with a list and a timeline.
S3.quote: I wouldn't want to have a baby the year both our jobs disappeared.
S3.fieldNote: Five years brings out her planner side, but she'd still follow proven paths rather than lead, watching where crew leader Dev goes. The most striking moment is her calm admission that she'd delay having children. She frames her choices around the couple, not herself alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and there's no excuse for being caught out. Everyone should have a plan by the halfway point. I'd probably say it at the depot and get told to stop being so organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's okay. I'd be thirty-seven, qualified, with a decade of experience and hopefully some savings for once. I'd have time to see what works for other people and then do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd qualify and get better with the planning software the office uses, since that's proven and it's already there. I'd keep saving, even small, and keep the wedding on track. Later on, around year four or five, I'd pick a direction based on who's still hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a manageable way. It feels like a deadline at work, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years let you do that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have the wedding, have a few good years, and choose instead of grab. With two years I'd be making lists at night, with ten I'd be making lists in daylight. That's a big difference to how you live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, still, because driving goes earlier and he hates sitting in classrooms. I'd want to help him find something with his hands, maybe fixing the robot vans. He's good with engines, so that might actually work.

S4.say: Ten years is fair warning and nobody has an excuse for being caught out; everyone should have a plan by the halfway point. She'd say it at the depot and be teased for being so organised.
S4.think: It's okay for her: at thirty-seven she'd be qualified, experienced and maybe have savings for once. She'd have time to see what works for others and copy it.
S4.do: Qualifies and gets better with the office's proven planning software in the first year. Keeps saving and keeps the wedding on track, then picks a direction around year four or five based on who's hiring.
S4.feel: Uneasy but manageable, like a work deadline rather than a disaster.
S4.quote: With two years I'd be making lists at night, with ten I'd be making lists in daylight.
S4.fieldNote: The warning time changes her emotionally more than practically: the plan is similar, but she'd live without dread. She'd still wait for proven paths and plans to choose a direction mid-decade. Her concern stays fixed on Marco, whom she imagines fixing the robot vans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits me and Marco at the same time and we've got nothing saved. What would help is something that keeps couples like us afloat for a year, so we don't lose the flat while we figure things out. And clear advice on which jobs are actually still there, from someone who knows.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the partner, not just the worker. Everyone thinks about one job, but households run on two. If you only look at mine, you'd think we'd be okay for a while, and we wouldn't be.

headlineQuote: Everyone thinks about one job, but households run on two.
portrait: Bianca Tanaka is a 27-year-old second-year apprentice connecting new housing estates to the network in a growing commuter town, carrying a notebook of knots, clearances and a budget with a mostly empty emergency line. She and her fiancé Marco, a delivery driver, are saving for a wedding on two low wages with about two weeks of money banked. She uses AI only for reports and adopts new tools once the crew has proven them. She's calm with a plateau and uneasy about steady change mostly because of Marco's job, then alarmed when AGI in two years would hit both of them at once. With more warning she'd shrink the wedding, delay children and follow colleagues into inspection work, always thinking as a household.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most because it would hit her and Marco at the same time with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Support that keeps couples afloat for a year so they don't lose their home, and clear advice from someone who knows which jobs are still there.
